title: Using the whole vegetable
description: Tops, stems, peels and bones of the vegetable world often carry as much flavour as the parts we usually keep.

body.heading: The parts we throw away too quickly
paragraphs: Carrot tops make a fine herby pesto or chimichurri. Broccoli stems, peeled, are sweet and crisp in stir-fries and salads. Cauliflower leaves roast into something between a crisp and a cabbage, and leek tops deepen any stock.
None of this requires adventurous eating. It is mostly about treating the whole plant as the ingredient you paid for, which, of course, it is.

body.heading: A jar of stock in the freezer
paragraphs: Keep a bag in the freezer for clean peelings, onion ends, herb stems and Parmesan rinds. When the bag is full, simmer it all in water for an hour, strain, and you have homemade stock for soups, risottos and grains at no cost.
Wash vegetables before peeling so the peelings are stock-worthy, and skip anything mouldy or from the cabbage family in large amounts, which can turn stock bitter.

body.heading: Citrus, herbs and stale bread
paragraphs: Lemon and orange zest freezes beautifully in a small jar and lifts cakes, dressings and pasta. Soft herbs heading past their best blend into sauces or freeze in ice-cube trays with a little oil.

Stale bread becomes croutons, breadcrumbs or a thickener for soups. The pattern is the same everywhere: a minute of imagination at the chopping board saves a surprising share of the weekly shop from the bin.

takeaway: Before you bin a stem, top or peel, ask whether it could be stock, sauce or supper, because often it can.
